extracted.intended_audience: emerging and established literary fiction writers; MFA students and creative-writing teachers
extracted.subtask_description: An interview offering practical craft guidance and editorial standards for writing and selecting literary short stories and novels, with attention to voice, humor, setting, narrative form, and editorial selection. Useful for fiction writers and teachers refining technique and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview conduct / verbal economy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Respond to questions directly and without unnecessary embellishment; when you don’t understand a question, say so; and if you don’t have an answer, don’t pretend that you do. Be generous with your time, but careful with your words. And if you can, if you have the confidence, wisdom, and artistry, be equal parts funny and mysterious."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice on how to comport oneself in an interview context; emphasizes directness, honesty about ignorance, economy of language, measured generosity, and a balance of humor and mystery. Although framed for interviews, this also implies values for written voice: clarity, economy, authenticity, and controlled wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin projects with a sense of urgency
rubrics_metrics.description: “I try to start a project with at least a small sense of urgency—one has to feel there is some reason for it, and something must propel it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A project should be motivated by a felt reason or propulsion; urgency supplies the drive to begin and carry the work forward. Lack of urgency may lead to drifting or lackluster work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist through intermittent lostness
rubrics_metrics.description: “One often continues work with an intermittent sense of lostness, despondency, and an inner voice chanting why why why. But that is merely falling down a little, and one gets back up and continues.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that feelings of doubt or despondency are part of the process; continued effort after these lapses is a key professional habit. This is practical advice about process and resilience rather than a stylistic rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate politics/world events authentically through characters
rubrics_metrics.description: “If by ‘politics’ you mean geo-political events, I have my usually very American characters sometimes intersect with them but more often just speak of them as American individuals would and did and continue to do.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including political or geopolitical material, let characters encounter and speak about events naturally, as their characters would, rather than forcing overt political messaging. Ground political material in character perspective and everyday speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the network of responsibility when addressing moral events
rubrics_metrics.description: “What I was interested in there is how large the network of responsibility might be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story engages ethically fraught events (e.g., Abu Ghraib), consider and dramatize the broader web of responsibility rather than offering simple individualizing judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mordant, paradoxical humor grounded in real speech
rubrics_metrics.description: “What draws me to humor is the mordant and paradoxical way people actually speak in times of worry and despair.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor dark, paradoxical, mordant humor that reflects how people actually speak under stress. Humor should arise from character and situation rather than being decorative or glib.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of language balanced by skepticism about language's limits
rubrics_metrics.description: “The book reflects a deep love of language—the clever puns and dark comedy, for which Moore first gained notice, persist—but the collection also reflects a suspicion that language’s recourses are limited in a world inured to panic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate attentive, clever use of language (puns, dark comedy) while remaining aware of the limits of linguistic gesture in representing or responding to large-scale suffering or panic; avoid relying on verbal cleverness to substitute for moral or emotional insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise setting (exact location and year)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Setting didn’t used to matter too much to me but now it matters completely. I need an exact location and an exact year in which my narrative is set and sometimes that shifts around while writing, which is stupid and disconcerting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about time and place—choose an exact location and year for the narrative. Specificity anchors the story and can change as the work develops, but aiming for precision helps shape detail and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by quality of the work, not by identity labels
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize the intrinsic nature and quality of the writing when evaluating work; resist letting an author’s label or identity substitute for judgments about the work itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous fragmentation; preserve narrative thread
rubrics_metrics.description: “I do occasionally try to discourage [fragments] in my students’ work … because sometimes a student’s fragments are a sign that they as authors have grown suddenly tired or self-contented, or have lost the narrative thread and have gotten on their phones to chat with their mothers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fragments are not inherently tied to gender and can be a legitimate technique, but beware of fragmentary prose that signals fatigue, self-satisfaction, or loss of narrative control. Use fragmentation deliberately and ensure it serves narrative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: precise, biting observations combined with vague, unfulfilled dreams
rubrics_metrics.description: “Her protagonists make precise and biting observations while harboring vague, unfulfilled dreams—a combination that reveals their complicity in an America becoming ever more bewildering.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft characters who can make sharp, specific observations even while their desires remain vague or unfulfilled; this tension can reveal complexities and complicity in larger social contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruthless selection and respect for historically 'stood out' work when editing anthologies
rubrics_metrics.description: “We had brutal space restraints that Updike didn’t have when he did his and it made the job kind of upsetting. We had great stories. They all stood out because they had stood out originally … but in the anniversary volume we had to whittle and whittle until we felt like we were cutting away at some of the vital organs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing anthologies, recognize space constraints and be prepared to make painful cuts; prioritize pieces that historically 'stood out' while accepting inevitable omissions. Selection requires both historical judgement and willingness to prune.
